english: Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and let $f:[-1,3]\setminus\{1\}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by
Suppose that $\lim_{x\to1}f(x)$ exists. Then the sum of all integers $m$ for which the equation $f(x)=m$ has at least one solution in $[-1,3]\setminus\{1\}$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $a\in\mathbb{R}$ तथा $f:[-1,3]\setminus\{1\}\to\mathbb{R}$ इस प्रकार परिभाषित है
माना कि $\lim_{x\to1}f(x)$ का अस्तित्व है। तब उन सभी पूर्णांकों $m$ का योग, जिनके लिए समीकरण $f(x)=m$ का $[-1,3]\setminus\{1\}$ में कम से कम एक हल है, ______ है।
solution: Limit exists at $1$ (removable, not infinite discontinuity) $\Rightarrow$ numerator vanishes at $1$: $1-3+a+5=0\Rightarrow a=-3$
On $[-1,1)$, $f$ is continuous and decreasing from $f(-1)=-2$ towards $-6$; on $(1,3]$ increasing from near $-6$ to $f(3)=-2$
By IVT every value in $(-6,-2]$ is taken; $-6$ (the limit at the removable discontinuity) is not taken
solution_full: As $x\to1$ the denominator tends to $0$. If the numerator tended to a non-zero value, $|f(x)|\to\infty$ (an infinite discontinuity) and the limit would not exist. So the numerator vanishes at $x=1$: $1-3+a+5=0$, giving $a=-3$.

Then $x^{3}-3x^{2}-3x+5=(x-1)(x^{2}-2x-5)$, so $f(x)=x^{2}-2x-5=(x-1)^{2}-6$ for $x\in[-1,3]$, $x\neq1$, and $\lim_{x\to1}f(x)=-6$. The discontinuity at $1$ is removable, but $1$ is not in the domain.

On $[-1,1)$: $f$ is continuous and strictly decreasing, $f(-1)=4-6=-2$, and $f(x)\to-6$ as $x\to1^{-}$. By the intermediate value theorem on $[-1,t]$ for $t<1$, $f$ takes every value in $[f(t),-2]$; letting $t\to1^{-}$, $f$ takes every value in $(-6,-2]$.
On $(1,3]$: similarly $f$ increases from values near $-6$ to $f(3)=4-6=-2$, giving the same set $(-6,-2]$.
The value $-6$ would need $(x-1)^{2}=0$, i.e. $x=1$, which is excluded. So the range of $f$ is $(-6,-2]$.
originality_note: New: the existence of the limit at a point outside the domain forces a removable discontinuity, and the missing value (the limit) is exactly the excluded end of the range, so the integer count must drop it; the rest of the range comes from the intermediate value theorem on each side (way 5). Closest known: choose a so that (x^3 + ...)/(x-1) has a limit at 1. Different because: the question turns the removable discontinuity into a range question where the missing value matters.
key_step: Limit exists means the numerator vanishes at 1, so f = (x-1)^2 - 6 off x = 1; the range is (-6, -2] with -6 missing.
justification: Routine chain: removable vs infinite discontinuity, factorisation, IVT for the range, and the excluded value. Similar length to 2025-P2-Q1 (L2); the trap at -6 keeps it at 2 rather than 1.

concept_use.Intermediate Value theorem: On [-1,1) and on (1,3], f is continuous and monotonic, so by the IVT it takes every value in (-6, -2].
concept_use.Types of discontinuity: A finite limit at x = 1 means the discontinuity is removable, not infinite, which forces a = -3; the limit value -6 is not attained.

stem_review: Read as a student: a and f (domain [-1,3] without 1, codomain) are defined; 'limit exists' is the only hypothesis; m ranges over integers and a solution must lie in the domain. Checked by sympy (factorisation) and a grid that the range is (-6, -2]. Answer -14, a negative integer. Changed: No change.
